summary: Module 2 CONTEXT micro-exercise: decompose 'add team invitations' into atomic tasks for this fork. Minimum six: (1) invitation data model -- Invitation table (id, team_id FK, inviter_id FK, invitee_email, token unique, status enum pending/accepted/revoked/expired, expires_at, used_at, accepted_by FK, created_at) + migration; (2) send-invitation endpoint -- POST /teams/{id}/invitations, auth + role check (owner/admin), rate-limited (fork pattern), schema-validated (pydantic, invitee_email format), returns 201 with the invite payload (not the token to the requester's discretion); (3) acceptance flow -- GET/POST accept endpoint keyed by one-time token, verifies token not used/expired, invitee identity matches the invitee_email (prevents unauthorized acceptance), creates TeamMember row, marks used_at, all in one transaction; (4) expiry handling -- pending invites with expires_at < now rejected by the accept endpoint and a periodic cleanup (mirrors fork's purge_old_clicks pattern); (5) revocation -- DELETE /teams/{id}/invitations/{invite_id} by owner/admin, status -> revoked, only while pending; (6) email notification -- send-on-invite via an email service integration. Edge cases to decide BEFORE prompting: invitee already a member (reject with 409), duplicate pending invite for same email+team (reject or idempotent-return existing), inviter loses admin between send and accept (accept still valid? decided: yes, because team membership was granted at send time; revocation is the admin's control), token replay (one-time use + used_at guard), token expiry race (checked in same transaction). Each task is atomic by the module's test: expected output describable in two sentences (e.g., 'POST /teams/{id}/invitations with a valid email returns 201 with the invitation and sets status=pending; a duplicate pending invite for the same email returns 409'), and verifiable without reading source. This decomposition converts the one-sentence spec into ~6 buildable units plus an edge-case matrix -- the 60% decomposition work that makes the 40% prompting/review cheap.
evidence: 6 atomic tasks enumerated with fork patterns (rate limit, pydantic, purge pattern, transaction semantics)
Edge-case matrix: duplicate invite, already-member, inviter admin loss, token replay, expiry race
Atomicity test applied: each task's acceptance criteria stateable in two sentences
